name: Ottoman Empire

areaKm2.note: world_1914 Ottoman Empire polygon = ~1.80M km2 computed on the sphere; B&H Table 2: 1.8M km2 (Turkey within present borders plus Syria, Palestine, Iraq and parts of Arabia).

population.note: Broadberry and Harrison 2005 Table 2: Ottoman Empire (present-day Turkey plus Syria, Palestine, Iraq and parts of Arabia) 1913 = 23.0M (high); B&H Table 9 (Urlanis) 21.7M; COW tpop 1913 = 21,331k, 1914 = 18,520k (low; the COW 1914 figure drops after the Balkan War losses were counted).

urbanization.note: HYDE (OWID) urban share Turkey 1910 = 17.3% (present-day Turkey). Mid 0.15 for the empire. Low = COW upop/tpop 1914 = 997/18,520 = 0.05 (cities over 100,000).

activePersonnel.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Erickson, Ordered to Die (isbn:0-313-31516-7), not read from a fetched source. Erickson, Ordered to Die ch. 1-2: mobilisation from 2 August 1914 raised the army from ~200,000 (COW milper 1914 = 249k) to ~800,000 by the time the empire entered the war (29 Oct-2 Nov 1914); many units were under strength. Navy ~10,000 and German Mittelmeerdivision crews (Goeben, Breslau) included. Snapshot month: November 1914.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Older mustahfiz reservists and Balkan War veterans not yet called; the army had lost many trained men in 1912-13.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Erickson, Ordered to Die (isbn:0-313-31516-7), not read from a fetched source. Artillery, depots, lines-of-communication troops (menzil), gendarmerie attached to the army, fortress artillery of the Straits, navy.

mobilizationRatio.note: Ottoman official figure (1922) and US War Dept on the cited page: 2,850,000 total mobilised; / ~21.5M = 0.13.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Erickson, Ordered to Die (isbn:0-313-31516-7), not read from a fetched source. ~36-38 infantry divisions in four armies by November 1914 (Erickson ch. 2), ~8,000-10,000 rifles each, plus frontier and jandarma battalions.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: Mauser rifles, few MGs, chronic shortages of boots and transport

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: Balkan War veterans and German-trained cadres; reservists poorly trained

count.note: Educated guess. Irregulars of the Teskilat-i Mahsusa and Arab tribal levies used as light infantry in late 1914.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: mixed rifles, no MGs or artillery

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25. Evidence: irregulars and tribal levies

count.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Erickson, Ordered to Die (isbn:0-313-31516-7), not read from a fetched source. Regular cavalry brigades plus Kurdish tribal (former Hamidiye) cavalry regiments on the Caucasus front.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: poorly mounted, tribal regiments unreliable

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: irregular cavalry

count.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Erickson, Ordered to Die (isbn:0-313-31516-7), not read from a fetched source. Krupp and Schneider field and mountain guns of ~36 divisions plus corps heavy artillery; Straits fortress guns excluded.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: modern Krupp QF guns, little heavy artillery outside the Dardanelles

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: German advisers trained the gunners

count.note: Educated guess. Ottoman aviation had only a handful of serviceable aircraft in late 1914; German-supplied machines arrived from 1915.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: a few Bleriot and Deperdussin types

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25. Evidence: a handful of pilots

count.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Conway's All the World's Fighting Ships 1906-1921 (isbn:0-85177-245-5), not read from a fetched source. Battleships, cruisers and destroyers. Yavuz Sultan Selim (ex-Goeben, battlecruiser), Midilli (ex-Breslau), 2 old Brandenburg-class battleships (Barbaros Hayreddin, Turgut Reis), the old Mesudiye, and cruisers Hamidiye and Mecidiye (Conway's; Ottoman Navy page) = 6/7/8; plus 4 Muavenet-class and 4 Samsun-class destroyers = 8. The two British-built dreadnoughts were seized by Britain in August 1914 (cited navy page). Role split per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries: destroyers moved from ships_minor.

quality.note: Count-weighted mean (mid counts) of battleships/cruisers 0.5/0.55/0.6 (7) and destroyers 0.4/0.45/0.5 (8), role split per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries. Rubric rows: quality 0.5 and 0.25-0.5. Evidence: Yavuz modern and the strongest ship in the Black Sea; the rest obsolete; small, old destroyers

training.note: Count-weighted mean (mid counts) of battleships/cruisers 0.5/0.55/0.6 (7) and destroyers 0.4/0.45/0.5 (8), role split per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries. Rubric rows: training 0.5 and 0.25-0.5. Evidence: German crews on Yavuz and Midilli, Ottoman crews weak; German-led after Aug 1914

count.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Conway's All the World's Fighting Ships 1906-1921 (isbn:0-85177-245-5), not read from a fetched source. A few large torpedo boats. The 8 destroyers (4 Muavenet, 4 Samsun class) moved to ships_major (was 8/10/12), role split per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: small, old destroyers

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: German-led after Aug 1914

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.5. Evidence: German advisers (Liman von Sanders) and capable officers (Mustafa Kemal) but Enver's Sarikamish offensive lost ~60,000-75,000 men in the winter of 1914-15

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.5. Evidence: Anatolian Turkish infantry tenacious in defence (Gallipoli); Arab and Kurdish units less reliable

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.5-0.75. Evidence: jihad proclamation and defence of the homeland; desertion grew from 1916

weapons.note: Anchor: 7 (1905). Evidence: Mauser rifles and Krupp QF guns, but few MGs and little heavy artillery

armor.note: Anchor: between 6 and 7. Evidence: no helmets or armoured vehicles

ships.note: Anchor: between 6 and 7 (dreadnoughts). Evidence: one modern battlecruiser (Yavuz), the rest pre-1890s ships

fortification.note: Anchor: 7 (concrete forts). Evidence: Dardanelles forts and minefields, Erzurum and Chatalja lines

logistics.note: Anchor: between 5 and 6 (magazines and requisition). Evidence: ~5,800 km of rail with gaps at the Taurus and Amanus tunnels; no rail to the Caucasus front; camel and porter transport

communications.note: Anchor: between 6 and 7 (telegraph). Evidence: telegraph network to the provinces; few telephones and radios

isr.note: Anchor: between 6 and 7 (aerial reconnaissance). Evidence: almost no aircraft in 1914

air.note: Anchor: between 6 and 7 (1914 aircraft). Evidence: a handful of aircraft

gdpPerCapita.note: B&H Table 2: 1,100 in 1990 int$. Maddison 2023 (OWID CSV, https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv) Turkey 1913 = 1,473 (2011 int$, present-day Turkey, high); the Arab provinces were poorer; scaling 1,100 by the Turkish 2011/1990 ratio (~1.2) gives ~1,350.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Defence absorbed roughly a third of the state budget before 1914 (~4% of GDP); wartime share constrained by a tiny tax base and German loans.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Industry and crafts ~10-15% of output; ~80% of the population in agriculture.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Formula: foodSurplus = 1 - agricultural share of employment. Agricultural share of employment assumed ~0.8 (no fetched occupational data for the empire).

annualCohort.note: Educated guess. Men reaching 20 per year in an empire of ~21M with high child mortality; Muslims only were conscripted in practice.

artillery.note: Educated guess. Field guns per year from the Tophane and Zeytinburnu works; almost all artillery came from Germany and Austria.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Engineered roads of Anatolia and the Arab provinces; most routes were tracks.

railKm.note: Educated guess. CHAT railline Turkey 1913 = 5,438 km (present-day Turkey, read from https://data.nber.org/chat/chat.dta, low); Syrian, Hejaz and Iraqi lines added from recollection.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Halpern, A Naval History of World War I (isbn:1-55750-352-4), not read from a fetched source. Constantinople, Smyrna, Beirut, Trebizond, Basra, Jaffa, Alexandretta.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Deadweight tons. The Ottoman steam fleet is not listed separately in Lloyd's 1914 returns; ~130,000 GRT (~200,000 dwt) assumed, comparable to the Turkish flag of 1929 (172,000 GRT, League of Nations table, https://www.istmat.org/files/uploads/49915/09_strany_mira_-_transport_torgovlya_platyozhnyy_balans.pdf).

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Ottoman armies operated at the end of very long animal-drawn lines (Sarikamish, Suez 1915); ~100 km beyond railheads.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. Horses, mules, camels and oxen of Anatolia and the Arab provinces.

homeDefense.note: 1.2 row: Straits fortifications, Anatolian plateau and population support; the 1.3 row applies on the Caucasus winter front (high).

notes: Snapshot date November 1914 (entry into the war 29 Oct-2 Nov 1914; mobilisation began 2 Aug). Territory = the empire after the Balkan Wars: Anatolia, Constantinople and eastern Thrace, Syria, Palestine, Iraq, Hejaz and Yemen (nominal); Egypt and Cyprus (British-occupied) and Libya excluded. Forces are the whole army; the Third Army in the Caucasus had ~100,000-150,000 men. Aircraft in aircraft_strike (no fighters). Ship convention per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries: battleships, carriers, cruisers and destroyers = ships_major, torpedo boats and smaller craft = ships_minor (role split per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries). Many values are reconstructions or educated guesses because Ottoman statistics are thin (Erickson is the main modern source, not fetched online).
